posts.title: Supervisor Agents: Orchestrating a Team of Specialists
posts.subtitle: One agent plans and delegates; others execute narrow, well-defined jobs.
posts.summary: Supervisor-worker orchestration splits a task between a planning agent that breaks work down and routes it, and specialist agents that execute narrow subtasks with their own tools and context. It trades single-agent simplicity for better focus and parallelism — at the cost of coordination overhead, extra token spend, and new failure modes at the handoffs.

slides.title: Why One Agent Isn't Always Enough
bullets: A single agent juggling research, coding, and writing tends to lose focus on long tasks
Supervisor-worker orchestration gives each subtask its own agent, tools, and context window
The tradeoff: more coordination, more tokens, more places for things to go wrong

slides.title: The Single-Agent Ceiling
slides.body: A lone agent's context window fills with everything at once — the original task, tool outputs, intermediate reasoning, and mistakes it's still correcting. Past a certain task complexity, relevant instructions get crowded out or the agent starts mixing up which sub-goal it's working on.
bullets: Long transcripts dilute the signal the model needs at each step
One noisy tool call (a huge search result, a giant stack trace) can crowd out everything else
Debugging is hard: it's unclear which part of a long run caused the failure

slides.title: The Pattern: A Supervisor That Delegates
slides.body: A supervisor agent holds the high-level goal and decomposes it into subtasks. Each subtask is handed to a specialist agent with its own clean context, its own tool access, and a narrow job — then reports a result back up.
bullets: Supervisor: plans, routes, and integrates results — usually doesn't touch raw tool output itself
Workers: narrow scope (e.g. 'search the codebase', 'draft the SQL', 'run the tests') with a fresh context each time
Handoffs pass a summary or structured result, not the worker's full transcript

slides.title: Sequential, Parallel, and Blackboard Variants
slides.body: Supervisor-worker isn't one fixed shape. Subtasks can run one after another when each depends on the last, fan out in parallel when they're independent, or post to a shared 'blackboard' that any agent can read and write for looser coordination.
bullets: Sequential: research agent -> writer agent -> reviewer agent, each depending on the prior output
Parallel: multiple specialist agents work independent subtasks simultaneously, supervisor merges results
Blackboard: agents share a common state store instead of passing messages directly — looser coupling, harder to trace

slides.title: Single Agent vs. Supervisor-Worker vs. Blackboard
bullets: More agents means more total tokens spent — orchestration isn't free just because it's parallel
The 'best' pattern is the least coordination that still fits the task's actual dependency structure

slides.title: Worked Example: Triaging a Support Ticket
slides.body: A supervisor receives a bug report. It routes to a 'reproduce' agent (runs the app, confirms the bug with fresh context), then a 'diagnose' agent (searches the codebase for the likely cause), then a 'fix' agent (writes the patch) — each getting only what it needs, not the full ticket thread.
bullets: Reproduce agent never sees the codebase search — it only needs steps to trigger the bug
Diagnose agent never sees the user's original message — it gets a clean bug description
Supervisor stitches the final summary from three short, focused reports instead of one sprawling transcript

slides.title: Where It Breaks Down
slides.body: Orchestration adds real overhead: every handoff risks losing nuance in the summary passed between agents, and splitting a task too finely multiplies API calls and latency without improving quality.
bullets: Over-fragmentation: subtasks so small that coordination costs exceed the work being coordinated
Lossy handoffs: a worker's caveat or edge case gets dropped when its result is summarized for the supervisor
Redundant work: parallel agents that aren't well-scoped end up solving overlapping pieces of the same problem
Not worth it for tasks a single well-scoped agent can already finish reliably

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: Split agents along task boundaries, not arbitrarily — each worker should have a job it can finish with a clean context
Sequential when subtasks depend on each other, parallel when they don't, blackboard only when coupling really is loose
Handoffs are the weak point: pass structured results, not vibes, between supervisor and workers
Add orchestration when a single agent's context is the bottleneck, not by default

questions.prompt: In a supervisor-worker setup, what does the supervisor typically do?
options: Executes every tool call itself alongside the workers
Plans, decomposes the task, routes subtasks to specialists, and integrates their results
Only monitors token usage and cost
Replaces the need for any specialist agents
questions.explanation: The supervisor holds the high-level goal and decomposition logic; specialist workers do the narrow execution with their own clean context and tools.

questions.prompt: What is the main risk of the 'blackboard' coordination pattern compared to supervisor-worker?
options: It requires far more tokens per agent than any other pattern
It cannot support parallel work at all
Looser, implicit coordination makes duplicate work and debugging harder to trace
It only works with a single agent
questions.explanation: Blackboard-style coordination trades explicit handoffs for a shared state any agent can read/write, which loosens coupling but makes it harder to know which agent did what and why.

questions.prompt: When is multi-agent orchestration NOT worth adding?
options: Whenever a task involves more than one tool call
When a single, well-scoped agent can already finish the task reliably within its context window
Only when the task is extremely long
Multi-agent orchestration should always be used for reliability
questions.explanation: Orchestration adds coordination cost, extra tokens, and lossy handoffs — worth it once single-agent context overload is the actual bottleneck, not as a default architecture.

posts.title: MCP Elicitation: Servers That Pause to Ask You Something
posts.subtitle: A standard way for an MCP tool to stop mid-task and request one missing piece of input, instead of guessing or failing.
posts.summary: Elicitation is the MCP capability that lets a server pause a running tool call and ask the human for one specific missing piece of information through a small, generic form — instead of guessing, failing, or asking the model to hallucinate a value. It keeps the exchange narrow (flat forms only) so any client can render it safely.

slides.title: MCP Elicitation: Servers That Pause to Ask You Something
slides.body: A tool call doesn't have to be all-or-nothing. Elicitation lets an MCP server stop mid-task, ask the human one concrete question, and resume with the answer.

slides.title: Before elicitation, a tool had two bad options
slides.body: When a tool call is missing a piece of information the model didn't provide, MCP servers used to have to pick between guessing and failing outright.
bullets: Guess a default and proceed — risky when the guess is wrong and the action has side effects (booking, sending, deleting)
Return an error and force the whole turn to restart — the model has to re-infer what was missing and re-issue the call
Neither path lets the server ask the actual human a direct, structured question in the middle of the call

slides.title: The server sends an elicitation request, the client renders a form
slides.body: Mid-call, the server sends an elicitation/create request back to the client: a short message string plus a requestedSchema describing exactly what it needs. The client shows that as a small form to the human, who accepts, declines, or cancels — and the tool call resumes with the answer.
bullets: The server is the one deciding it needs more input, not the model — it's a protocol-level pause, not a prompt trick
The human sees a purpose-built form, not raw JSON or a chat message they have to interpret
The response is one of three actions: accept (with data), decline, or cancel — the server must handle all three

slides.title: Why the schema is deliberately kept flat
slides.body: requestedSchema is restricted to a flat object of primitive fields — strings, numbers, booleans, and enums. No nested objects, no arrays of objects. That's not a limitation of the format; it's the whole point.
bullets: A flat schema means any client can render it generically as a simple form, without custom UI per server
It also caps what a server can ask for in one shot — nothing that resembles a multi-page onboarding flow
Clients are expected to show which server is asking, so the human always knows who's requesting the data

slides.title: A flight-booking tool that needs a seat preference
slides.body: The model calls a book_flight tool with the route and dates, but the user never mentioned a seat preference and the tool needs one to complete the booking.
bullets: The server pauses the call and sends an elicitation request: 'Which seat would you like?' with an enum field — window, aisle, no preference
The client renders that as three tappable options instead of dumping the question back into the chat transcript
The user taps 'aisle,' the server receives an accept response with { seat: "aisle" }, and the booking call completes with real data instead of a guess

slides.title: Elicitation vs. the other MCP client capabilities
slides.body: MCP gives servers three distinct ways to reach back into the client — each for a different job.

headers: What it asks the client for
rows: One piece of structured input, via a flat form
An LLM completion, using the client's model
Which filesystem/URI boundaries the server may touch
Set once by the client, not per-call

slides.title: When to reach for elicitation — and when not to
slides.body: Elicitation is for one missing, well-defined input — not a substitute for good tool design or a way around trust boundaries.
bullets: Good fit: a single missing parameter with real consequences if guessed wrong (destination, confirmation, a choice among options)
Bad fit: asking for secrets or credentials — the spec expects clients to warn or refuse if a server tries to elicit sensitive data like passwords
Don't use it to paper over a poorly scoped tool that should have just asked for the parameter up front
Every elicitation call needs a real fallback path for decline/cancel — a server that only handles 'accept' will hang or crash on a 'no'

questions.prompt: What problem does MCP elicitation solve that plain tool calls can't?
options: It makes tool calls run faster by skipping validation
It lets a server pause mid-call to ask the human for one specific missing piece of input, instead of guessing or failing
It replaces the need for a JSON schema on tool arguments entirely
It lets the server call other tools without the client's involvement
questions.explanation: Before elicitation, a server missing a required input could only guess a default or return an error. Elicitation adds a protocol-level pause where the server asks the human directly and resumes with the answer.

questions.prompt: Why is requestedSchema restricted to a flat object of primitive fields (strings, numbers, booleans, enums)?
options: Because nested objects aren't valid JSON
So any client can render the request as a generic form without custom per-server UI, and so servers can't smuggle in a large multi-step form
Because the MCP spec doesn't support JSON Schema at all
To make the response smaller over the wire for bandwidth reasons
questions.explanation: Keeping the schema flat means every client can render a consistent, simple form generically, and it caps how much a single elicitation can ask for — it's a deliberate scope limit, not a technical accident.

questions.prompt: A user is shown an elicitation form and taps 'Cancel.' What must the server do?
options: Retry the same elicitation request automatically until the user accepts
Treat it as equivalent to an empty string answer and proceed anyway
Handle it as a real outcome distinct from 'accept' — the tool call needs a defined path for decline/cancel, not just the happy path
Crash, since cancel is not a valid MCP response
questions.explanation: Elicitation responses are one of accept, decline, or cancel. A server that only implements the accept path will hang or misbehave the first time a user says no — decline/cancel handling isn't optional.

posts.title: SpatialBlock: Block-Stacking Puzzles Teach AI to See in 3D
posts.subtitle: 15,000 synthetic block puzzles beat specialist models trained on real scenes.
posts.summary: A new paper (arXiv:2609.07064) shows large vision-language models can learn real-world 3D spatial reasoning from a synthetic dataset of just 15,000 block-stacking puzzles. Models trained on SpatialBlock-15k beat prior specialist baselines on real-scene spatial benchmarks — the 3B variant beats SOTA model SpatialLadder by 2.7%, and the 7B variant beats SpaceR and Spatial-SSRL, despite using far less training data.

slides.title: LVLMs Can Describe a Photo but Can't Rebuild Its Geometry
bullets: Vision-language models ace captioning and object recognition
Ask them to reconstruct a scene's 3D layout from a 2D image and they falter
A new paper trains that skill using synthetic toy blocks, not real photos

slides.title: Spatial Reasoning Is the Blind Spot Benchmarks Keep Finding
slides.body: Large vision-language models (LVLMs) are trained mostly on natural images paired with text, which teaches recognition but not geometry. Ask one to predict what a scene looks like from a rotated viewpoint, or to reconstruct which object is behind which, and accuracy drops sharply.
bullets: 3D-to-2D projection, viewpoint change, and object-relation structure are all weak points
Real-world spatial-reasoning datasets are expensive to collect and hard to label precisely
Prior fixes (SpatialLadder, SpaceR, Spatial-SSRL) needed much larger, real-scene training sets

slides.title: Train on Block-Stacking Instead of Real Scenes
slides.body: The authors' insight: human children build spatial intuition through block play long before they reason about real rooms. SpatialBlock mimics that with a synthetic curriculum.
bullets: SpatialBlock-15k: 15,000 synthetic block-stacking problems, fully auto-generated
Covers three skills: 3D-to-2D projection, viewpoint transformation, structural combination
Controlled color modulation on blocks gives the model a visual anchor to reason from
Models are trained either to answer directly or to produce a reasoning chain before answering

slides.title: Why Synthetic Blocks Generalize to Real Rooms
slides.body: Block-stacking isolates the underlying geometric operations (projection, rotation, occlusion) from the visual noise of real scenes, so the model learns the operation itself rather than scene-specific shortcuts.
bullets: Synthetic generation means precise, noise-free ground-truth labels at scale
Color-coded blocks act as anchors — the model tracks 'the red block' through a viewpoint change
Because the task family (projection, rotation, structure) is general, the learned skill transfers

slides.title: Small Data, Beats Bigger Specialist Baselines
Worked Example: The Hidden Block Problem
slides.body: A concrete case shows what the model is actually learning.
bullets: Input: a photo of three colored blocks stacked, viewed from the front
Question: 'If you viewed this from the left side, which block would be hidden?'
The model uses the color anchors to track each block's identity through the imagined rotation
It answers by reasoning about occlusion under the new viewpoint — not by pattern-matching pixels

slides.title: Where the Trick Could Break Down
slides.body: Training entirely on a narrow synthetic domain is a bet, not a guarantee.
bullets: Blocks are a simplified proxy — cluttered, irregular real-world objects add complexity blocks don't have
Real-scene benchmark gains are reported, but block-stacking is still a narrow task family
Color-anchor reasoning may not transfer cleanly to scenes without clear color-coded cues
It's a training-data trick, not an architecture change — it doesn't fix a model with no spatial capacity

slides.title: The Takeaway: Curriculum Design Can Beat Raw Scale
bullets: SpatialBlock-15k is 100% synthetic, auto-generated, and still beats real-scene-trained baselines
The core idea: isolate the geometric skill (projection, rotation, structure) from visual noise
3B model beats SOTA SpatialLadder by 2.7%; 7B model beats SpaceR and Spatial-SSRL
A well-designed small dataset can out-teach a larger, noisier one

questions.prompt: What is the core weakness in LVLMs that SpatialBlock targets?
options: Poor image captioning accuracy
Weak 3D spatial reasoning — reconstructing scene geometry from 2D images
Slow inference speed on mobile devices
Inability to process color images
questions.explanation: LVLMs are strong at recognition and captioning but struggle with 3D-to-2D projection, viewpoint changes, and object-relation structure — the geometric reasoning SpatialBlock trains.

questions.prompt: Why does SpatialBlock use synthetic block-stacking puzzles instead of real photos?
options: Real photos are copyrighted and can't be used for training
Blocks isolate the geometric operations from real-scene visual noise, giving cleaner training signal
Synthetic data trains faster on any hardware
Block images compress to a smaller file size
questions.explanation: By stripping away real-world visual clutter, the synthetic block tasks let the model learn the underlying geometric operation (projection, rotation, occlusion) directly, which then transfers to real scenes.

questions.prompt: How did the SpatialBlock-trained 3B model compare to the prior state-of-the-art SpatialLadder?
options: It performed 2.7% worse
It matched it exactly
It outperformed it by 2.7%, despite training on only 15K synthetic samples
It was not compared to SpatialLadder
questions.explanation: Despite the compact, fully synthetic training set, the Qwen-based 3B SpatialBlock model beat SpatialLadder — the prior state-of-the-art trained on larger real-scene data — by 2.7% on real-scene spatial benchmarks.

posts.title: Gemini 3.8 Flash Cyber: Google's Gated Vulnerability Hunter
posts.subtitle: A model good enough to find bugs everywhere is exactly why Google won't give it to everyone.
posts.summary: Google DeepMind released Gemini 3.8 Flash Cyber, a cybersecurity-specialized model paired with its CodeMender patching agent, and launched the Fairwind Program to gate access to vetted defenders — government agencies, critical-infrastructure operators, and cybersecurity partners. Google reports 70%+ internal vulnerability-discovery accuracy across 20 languages, 2.6x more correct Chrome patches than leading commercial models, and 47.2% pass@1 on CWE-Bench.

slides.title: The Best Bug-Finder Is Also the Best Exploit-Writer
bullets: Google shipped its most capable vulnerability-hunting model yet: Gemini 3.8 Flash Cyber
It isn't available to everyone who wants it
A new vetting program called Fairwind decides who gets in

slides.title: Cybersecurity AI Is Inherently Dual-Use
slides.body: A model skilled at finding software vulnerabilities is, by construction, also skilled at finding ways to exploit them. Publishing weights or opening a public API for a top-tier vulnerability scanner risks arming attackers as much as defenders.
bullets: Frontier-level bug-hunting capability can't be safely shipped the way a chat model can
Open access would help defenders patch faster — but also help attackers find zero-days faster
Google's answer: keep the capability real, but control who can reach it

slides.title: Gemini 3.8 Flash Cyber + Fairwind: Capability Paired With Gatekeeping
slides.body: Instead of a public release, Google paired the model with its CodeMender remediation agent and built a partner-vetting program around it.
bullets: Gemini 3.8 Flash Cyber pairs with CodeMender, Google's AI agent for vulnerability remediation
Fairwind Program grants access only to vetted defenders: government agencies, Google Cloud customers, cybersecurity partners
Priority goes to critical-infrastructure operators and maintainers of widely used software
Access requires organizational vetting, multi-factor authentication, and role restriction to security staff (incident response, pen testing, etc.)

slides.title: A Partner Network, Not Just a Model
slides.body: Fairwind is built as an ecosystem, not a single API key.
bullets: Google says it's working with 650+ partners globally
Named partners include CrowdStrike, Datadog, Menlo Security, Palo Alto Networks, and Snowflake
The program targets defenders who need early access to advanced capability before new threats emerge

slides.title: The Headline Numbers

rows: Chrome patch correctness vs. leading commercial models

slides.title: Worked Scenario: Triaging a Fuzzer Crash
slides.body: A concrete picture of the intended workflow.
bullets: A fuzzer finds a crash in a widely used open-source library
A vetted security team feeds the crash report to Gemini 3.8 Flash Cyber for root-cause analysis
CodeMender proposes a candidate patch; the model's accuracy claims (2.6x more correct Chrome patches) apply here
A human reviewer on the vetted team still validates before merging — access control doesn't remove the review step

slides.title: Tradeoffs of the Gated Approach
slides.body: Access control solves one problem and creates others.
bullets: Most independent developers and smaller open-source maintainers can't get in — only vetted orgs and partners
Google isn't alone in this pattern this cycle: Anthropic's Mythos 5.1 and OpenAI's Astra also ship cyber capability behind trusted-access tiers
Vetting and MFA reduce but don't eliminate misuse risk if a vetted account is compromised
It signals a broader industry shift: safety is increasingly enforced via who can access a model, not just how the model itself is trained

slides.title: The Takeaway
bullets: Gemini 3.8 Flash Cyber is Google's most capable cybersecurity model to date, paired with the CodeMender patching agent
The Fairwind Program gates access to vetted defenders — 650+ partners, priority to critical infrastructure
Reported results: 70%+ vulnerability discovery, 2.6x more correct Chrome patches, 47.2% on CWE-Bench
Access-gating alongside capability release is becoming the industry's default move for dual-use AI

questions.prompt: Why did Google restrict access to Gemini 3.8 Flash Cyber instead of releasing it publicly?
options: The model isn't ready for production use
A model powerful at finding vulnerabilities is equally powerful at finding exploits — it's dual-use
Google wants to charge a premium price for it
The model only works on Google's own infrastructure
questions.explanation: Vulnerability-discovery skill is dual-use by nature: the same capability that helps defenders patch bugs faster helps attackers find and exploit them. Gating access is Google's mitigation.

questions.prompt: What does the Fairwind Program actually control?
options: The model's pricing tiers
Which organizations and individuals can access Gemini 3.8 Flash Cyber and CodeMender
How many tokens a request can use
Which programming languages the model supports
questions.explanation: Fairwind is an access-vetting program: it grants entry to government agencies, Google Cloud customers, and cybersecurity partners, with priority to critical-infrastructure operators, and requires MFA and role restrictions.

questions.prompt: What does the 2.6x figure refer to in Google's reported results?
options: 2.6x faster inference speed
2.6x more correct patches delivered to Chrome vulnerabilities than leading commercial models
2.6x more partners than last year's program
2.6x reduction in false positives
questions.explanation: Google reports Gemini 3.8 Flash Cyber, paired with CodeMender, delivers 2.6x more correct patches to Chrome vulnerabilities compared to leading commercial models — a patch-quality metric, not a speed metric.

posts.title: State Space Models: The Architecture That Skips Attention
posts.subtitle: Constant memory per token, no quadratic blowup — but it has to relearn what attention gave away for free.
posts.summary: State space models (SSMs) like Mamba process sequences as a recurrent linear dynamical system instead of computing pairwise attention, giving O(n) compute and constant memory per step at inference. Mamba's key trick — making the recurrence's parameters input-dependent — lets it selectively remember or forget tokens, closing much of the gap with attention while staying linear in sequence length.

slides.title: What If a Language Model Never Looked Back?
bullets: Transformers attend to every previous token, every layer, every step
That's powerful — and it's O(n²) compute, O(n) memory that keeps growing
State space models process text as a recurrence instead — and Mamba made that competitive

slides.title: Attention's Bill Comes Due at Long Context
slides.body: Self-attention computes a score between every pair of tokens, so both compute and the KV cache scale with sequence length — quadratically for compute, linearly (but with real memory pressure) for the cache. Long documents, long conversations, and long agent traces all pay this tax.
bullets: Compute for one layer of attention scales as O(n²) in sequence length n
The KV cache that makes autoregressive decoding fast still scales as O(n) — and it's the thing that blows up GPU memory at long context
Techniques like PagedAttention and MLA manage that cache better; they don't remove the underlying scaling

slides.title: The State Space Model Alternative: A Recurrence, Not a Lookup
slides.body: An SSM keeps a fixed-size hidden state and updates it one token at a time using linear algebra, much like a classic control-theory system.
bullets: At each step: new_state = A · state + B · input, output = C · state
A, B, C are learned matrices; the state has fixed size regardless of how long the sequence gets
Compute per token is O(1) at inference, and memory doesn't grow with sequence length — no KV cache at all
During training, the same recurrence can be computed in parallel via a convolution or scan, so it's not forced to run token-by-token

slides.title: Mamba's Fix: Make the Recurrence Data-Dependent
slides.body: Earlier SSMs (like S4) used fixed A, B, C matrices for every input — good at long-range smoothing, bad at content-based reasoning. Mamba's 'selective SSM' changes that.
bullets: In Mamba, B, C, and the update rate are computed from the current input token itself
That lets the model choose, per token, what to let into the state and what to let decay out
It's the SSM analogue of attention's 'look at what's relevant' — but folded into a recurrence, not a pairwise score
A hardware-aware parallel scan algorithm keeps this selective version fast on GPUs despite being input-dependent

slides.title: SSM vs. Attention: What Each Is Actually Good At

rows: Weaker — bottlenecked through a fixed-size state

slides.title: Worked Example: Streaming a 100K-Token Log File
slides.body: A concrete comparison of what happens at inference time.
bullets: A Transformer processing a 100K-token log must keep a KV cache entry for every one of those tokens to attend back to them
A Mamba-style model compresses everything seen so far into one fixed-size state vector, updated token by token
Memory footprint for the SSM stays flat as the log grows; the Transformer's keeps climbing
The tradeoff: if the answer depends on recalling one exact rare token from far back, the SSM's compressed state may have already discarded it

slides.title: Where Pure SSMs Fall Short
slides.body: Compressing history into a fixed-size state is a lossy operation, and that loss shows up on specific task types.
bullets: Tasks needing exact copying or precise retrieval of a specific earlier token (e.g. 'repeat the 6-digit code from earlier') are harder for a compressed state than for attention's direct lookup
Because of this, most production long-context systems now use hybrid stacks — a few attention layers interleaved with many SSM layers — rather than pure SSMs
SSM kernels are newer and less standardized than attention kernels, so tooling and hardware support are less mature
Don't reach for a pure SSM when the task is dominated by needle-in-haystack retrieval; do reach for one when the task is long-context throughput at bounded memory

slides.title: The Takeaway
bullets: SSMs trade attention's pairwise lookups for a recurrence with a fixed-size hidden state — O(n) compute, constant inference memory
Mamba's selective mechanism makes that recurrence input-dependent, closing much of the quality gap with attention
The real-world answer is usually hybrid: mix a few attention layers with many SSM layers, not one or the other
Pick based on the task: long-context throughput favors SSMs; exact retrieval still favors attention

questions.prompt: What is the main computational advantage of a state space model over standard self-attention?
options: It uses less training data
It achieves O(n) compute and constant inference memory instead of attention's O(n²) compute and growing KV cache
It requires no GPU to run
It produces higher-resolution outputs
questions.explanation: SSMs replace pairwise attention scores with a fixed-size recurrent state, so compute scales linearly with sequence length and inference memory stays constant — no KV cache that grows with context.

questions.prompt: What did Mamba change compared to earlier state space models like S4?
options: It removed the recurrence entirely and used only attention
It made the recurrence's parameters (B, C, update rate) depend on the current input, enabling selective memory
It increased the fixed state size to match sequence length
It eliminated the need for any hidden state
questions.explanation: Earlier SSMs like S4 used fixed A, B, C matrices for every input. Mamba's 'selective SSM' computes B, C, and the update rate from the current token, letting the model choose what to remember or forget per token.

questions.prompt: Why do most production long-context systems use hybrid Mamba-Transformer stacks rather than pure SSMs?
options: Pure SSMs are too slow to train
Pure SSMs compress history into a fixed-size state, which is lossy and hurts tasks needing exact token retrieval
Hybrid stacks are cheaper to license
Attention layers are required for tokenization
questions.explanation: A fixed-size state can't perfectly preserve every earlier token, so pure SSMs underperform on exact-copying or needle-in-haystack retrieval tasks. Interleaving a few attention layers recovers that capability while keeping most of the SSM's efficiency.

posts.title: Ternary LLMs: The 1.6-Bit Assumption Was Wrong
posts.subtitle: 29 models later, zeros turn out to be the real payload.
posts.summary: A new paper (arXiv:2609.16338) shows the standard 1.6-bit-per-weight packing format for ternary LLMs wastes space by assuming a uniform {-1,0,+1} distribution. Measuring 29 real models found zeros can hit 51.5% of weights; a new layout called BITCOS reads each model's own zero fraction to shrink storage further and speed up inference — with no retraining.

slides.title: Every Ternary Weight Costs 1.6 Bits — Except It Doesn't
bullets: Ternary LLMs store each weight as -1, 0, or +1
The textbook floor is log2(3) ≈ 1.585 bits/weight
A new paper shows real models beat that floor — legally

slides.title: The Packing Format Everyone Uses Wastes Bits
slides.body: Ternary weight-2 formats are popular for on-device and edge deployment because {-1,0,+1} needs far less storage than int8 or fp16. But the standard deployment format bakes in an assumption nobody had actually checked.
bullets: Standard format packs 5 ternary weights per byte ("5-trit packing")
8 bits / 5 trits = 1.6 bits/weight in theory, 1.625 in practice after power-of-two group-size rounding
That format assumes -1, 0, and +1 are roughly equally likely — a guess, not a measurement

slides.title: Zeros Aren't 1/3 of the Weights — They're Half
slides.body: The authors measured the actual symbol distribution across 29 published ternary LLMs instead of assuming one.
bullets: Measured 29 real trained ternary models, not synthetic weight draws
Zero fraction varied widely — up to 51.5% of all weights in the sparsest models
That skew means the uniform 1.585-bit theoretical floor never actually applied to real checkpoints

slides.title: BITCOS: A Bitmap for 'Is It Zero,' a Vector for the Sign
slides.body: BITCOS splits storage into two structures instead of one fixed-width code per weight.
bullets: Layer 1: a dense presence bitmap — 1 bit per weight, marks zero vs nonzero
Layer 2: a compacted sign vector — stores +/- only for the nonzero entries
Total cost: 2 − z bits/weight, where z is that model's own measured zero fraction
No retraining, no new checkpoint — same trained weights, a smarter on-disk/on-GPU layout

slides.title: The Numbers: Same Weights, Denser Layout

rows: No — adapts to each model's zero fraction

slides.title: What ~9% Smaller Looks Like on a Real-Sized Model
slides.body: Applying the paper's reported bits/weight figures to a hypothetical model makes the savings concrete.
bullets: Take a hypothetical 70B-parameter ternary model with z = 0.515 (matching the paper's sparsest case)
Old 5-trit packing: 1.625 bits/weight → ~14.2GB just for weight storage
BITCOS at 2 − z = 1.485 bits/weight → ~13.0GB, roughly 9% smaller
Same accuracy, same checkpoint — only the storage layout changed

slides.title: The Catch: Gains Depend on How Sparse Your Model Already Is
slides.body: BITCOS isn't a universal win — it's a bet on a property some models have more of than others.
bullets: Savings scale with z — a model with few zero weights barely benefits from this scheme
The bitmap decode adds a small per-access branch; gains show up in throughput, not just raw size
Only applies to true ternary {-1,0,+1} weights — doesn't transfer to int4/int8/fp8 quantization
It's a storage/inference trick, not a training-time fix — it can't rescue a badly-quantized model

slides.title: The Takeaway: Your Quantized Model Was Already Compressible Further
bullets: Ternary LLMs were never uniformly distributed — assuming so wasted real bits in every deployment
BITCOS reads a model's own zero fraction and encodes accordingly: 2 − z bits/weight
On the sparsest of 29 tested models: ~1.485 bits/weight, 1.18x-1.27x faster inference
It's a free lunch only because it's decoding reality, not changing the model

questions.prompt: What is the information-theoretic minimum for storing a ternary weight, assuming -1, 0, and +1 are equally likely?
options: 1 bit
log2(3) ≈ 1.585 bits
2 bits
4 bits
questions.explanation: log2(3) ≈ 1.585 bits/weight is the Shannon-optimal cost IF all three symbols are equally likely. BITCOS's whole insight is that in real trained models, they usually aren't.

questions.prompt: Why does the standard '5 trits per byte' packing format cost 1.625 bits/weight instead of the theoretical 1.6?
options: Because ternary weights need an extra sign bit
Because power-of-two group sizes round the packing up in practice
Because zeros are stored using two bits each
Because GPUs require every format to be byte-aligned
questions.explanation: 8 bits / 5 trits = 1.6 bits/weight in theory, but real deployments use power-of-two group sizes for the packed blocks, which rounds the effective cost up to 1.625 bits/weight.

questions.prompt: What does BITCOS exploit that the standard packing format ignores?
options: That most models are trained on synthetic data
That zeros make up a much larger, non-uniform share of ternary weights than assumed
That GPUs multiply faster than they add
That weights change after a model is deployed
questions.explanation: Measuring 29 real ternary LLMs showed zeros can be up to 51.5% of weights — far from the ~33% a uniform distribution would predict. BITCOS's bitmap-plus-sign-vector layout directly encodes that skew instead of ignoring it.

posts.title: HNSW: How Vector Search Finds Neighbors Fast
posts.subtitle: Skip lists met graphs, and approximate nearest-neighbor search got fast.
posts.summary: HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small World) is the graph-based index behind most production vector databases. By searching a multi-layer proximity graph instead of scanning every vector, it turns nearest-neighbor lookup from an O(n) scan into roughly O(log n) hops — at the cost of approximate (not exact) results and real memory overhead.

slides.title: Searching a Billion Vectors Without Checking Each One
bullets: Brute-force nearest-neighbor search checks every vector: O(n) per query
HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small World) answers in roughly O(log n)
It's the default index behind most production vector databases today

slides.title: The Problem: Exact Nearest Neighbor Doesn't Scale
slides.body: For RAG, every query embedding must be compared against millions of stored vectors to find the closest matches. Exact brute-force comparison is linear — fine at small scale, unworkable at real scale.
bullets: Brute-force cosine/dot-product search compares the query to every stored vector
At 10M vectors and 768 dimensions, that's ~10M dot products per query
Latency scales linearly with corpus size — doubling your data doubles every query's cost

slides.title: The Trick: A 'Skip List' Made of Graphs
slides.body: HNSW builds several layers of a proximity graph. The top layer has very few nodes with long-range links; each layer below has progressively more nodes with shorter links, down to the bottom layer containing every vector.
bullets: Every vector is a node in the bottom (densest) layer
Higher layers contain a random, shrinking subset of nodes — fewer nodes, longer edges
Search starts at the sparse top layer, greedily walks toward the query, drops a layer, repeats
Each layer narrows the search region before the next does finer-grained work

slides.title: Why It's Fast: Logarithmic Hops, Not Linear Scans
slides.body: Two tunable parameters control the accuracy/speed tradeoff directly.
bullets: Search cost is roughly O(log n) hops through the graph, not O(n) comparisons
Insertion is also O(log n): a new vector picks a random max layer, then greedily connects to nearby nodes at each layer it belongs to
M controls max connections per node; efSearch/efConstruction controls how wide the greedy search explores
Higher ef = better recall, more comparisons per query — a direct accuracy/latency dial

slides.title: HNSW vs. the Alternatives
Tuning HNSW for a 5M-Document RAG Index
slides.body: A concrete parameter choice for a mid-size production index.
bullets: 5M chunk embeddings at 1536 dimensions (a typical embedding model's output size)
M=16 (moderate connectivity), efConstruction=200 for the build pass
efSearch=64 at query time → sub-20ms p99 latency in typical vector-DB benchmarks, ~97% recall@10
Bump efSearch to 128 to chase 99% recall — latency roughly doubles, still far below brute-force

slides.title: When HNSW Is the Wrong Choice
bullets: Recall is approximate, never guaranteed exact — wrong tool if you need provably-correct top-k
The index is memory-hungry: graph edges add real overhead on top of raw vector storage
Insertions are cheap; bulk deletes aren't — most implementations mark-and-skip rather than truly remove nodes, bloating the graph over time
For small corpora (under ~100K vectors), brute-force can be just as fast and far simpler to reason about

slides.title: The Takeaway
bullets: HNSW trades exact recall for logarithmic-time approximate search via a multi-layer graph
M and ef are the real levers: more connections and wider search mean higher recall at higher cost
It's the default ANN index in most production vector databases for a reason — but not free at scale (memory) or under heavy deletes
For RAG at real scale, HNSW is usually the right default; validate recall@k on your own embeddings before trusting it blindly

questions.prompt: What is the primary reason HNSW is faster than brute-force nearest-neighbor search?
options: It compresses vectors before comparing them
It searches a multi-layer graph greedily instead of comparing to every vector
It only searches vectors uploaded in the last 24 hours
It uses GPU parallelism exclusively
questions.explanation: HNSW's speed comes from its layered graph structure: a sparse top layer narrows the search region quickly, then denser lower layers refine it — turning an O(n) scan into roughly O(log n) hops.

questions.prompt: What does increasing the efSearch parameter do?
options: Deletes low-quality vectors from the index
Widens the greedy search at query time, trading latency for higher recall
Reduces the number of graph layers
Compresses the vector dimensions
questions.explanation: efSearch controls how many candidates HNSW explores per layer during a query. Higher ef means more comparisons (slower) but a better chance of finding the true nearest neighbors (higher recall).

questions.prompt: Why is HNSW a poor fit for an index with frequent bulk deletions?
options: It cannot store more than 1 million vectors
Most implementations mark deleted nodes rather than truly removing them, bloating the graph over time
Deleting a vector requires rebuilding all layers from scratch every time
HNSW indexes cannot be updated after creation
questions.explanation: HNSW graphs are built incrementally and optimized for insertion, not removal. Cleanly deleting a node would require re-linking its neighbors, so most implementations just mark it deleted and skip it during search — leaving dead weight in the graph until a full rebuild.

posts.title: Recursive Self-Improvement: Five Stages of AI Autonomy
posts.subtitle: A 33-author roadmap for AI that improves how it improves — and why we're only at stage 3
posts.summary: A large multi-institution paper proposes a 5-stage taxonomy for recursive self-improvement in AI, from a system that executes a fix it's told to make, up to one that revises its own improvement process. Current systems demonstrably reach stages 1-3; nobody has shown a stage-5 case where a self-revised improvement method fairly beats the original.

slides.title: "Self-improving AI" is a headline, not a measurement
slides.body: A September 2026 paper from researchers at Shanghai Jiao Tong University, Tsinghua, ByteDance, and Shanghai AI Lab tries to fix that by breaking recursive self-improvement (RSI) into five concrete, checkable stages.
bullets: 33 authors, trending #1 on Hugging Face Daily Papers
arXiv 2609.11873, posted Sep 10, 2026

slides.title: Every lab claims 'self-improvement' — for different things
slides.body: A model that fixes a bug when told to, and a model that decides what to fix, gather its own training data, and rewrite its own learning algorithm, get lumped under the same buzzword. That makes real progress impossible to compare.
bullets: RSI = turning experience/feedback into persistent changes that improve both capability AND the process of future improvement
The gap between 'runs an optimization loop' and 'owns the optimization loop' is the whole ballgame
Without stages, every autocomplete-a-patch demo gets marketed as 'AI improving itself'

slides.title: The roadmap: five autonomy stages, each removing one human dependency
slides.body: Each stage keeps everything from the prior stage but hands the AI one more decision that used to require a person.
bullets: 1. Improvement-Execution: AI carries out a fix once told exactly what to fix
2. Improvement-Strategy: AI diagnoses the weakness and picks which intervention to try; objectives/eval still set by humans
3. Experience-Acquisition: AI goes and gathers the experience it needs instead of waiting to be fed a dataset
4. Environment-Adaptation: AI adjusts to conditions it wasn't originally set up for
5. Recursive Meta-Improvement: AI improves the improvement process itself — the loop closes

slides.title: Where the frontier actually sits today

rows: Choosing what to fix and how

slides.title: A stage-2 case study: an agent that revises its own patch strategy
slides.body: The paper points to software-engineering agents that, when a bug-fix strategy underperforms, autonomously switch to a different search strategy (e.g., from local patch-and-test to tracing the call graph first) — without a human rewriting its prompt.
bullets: That's improvement-strategy autonomy (stage 2): the AI picked the intervention, but success/failure was still graded by a human-defined test suite
Researchers found cases where an AI revised its own improvement method and the revision got adopted
But no case where that revised method was shown to reliably outperform the original under a fair, controlled comparison — the key stage-5 bar

slides.title: Why stage 5 is so hard to prove — not just build
slides.body: The bottleneck isn't only capability. It's measurement.
bullets: A 'fair test' requires isolating the revised improvement process from the capability gains it produced — easy to conflate
Self-play and synthetic-experience loops can silently overfit to their own generator, inflating scores without generalizing
Scenarios differ wildly in how fast they can climb the ladder: software engineering moves faster than embodied robotics or wet-lab science, because feedback is cheap and simulatable

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: RSI isn't one thing — it's five separable, individually-checkable capabilities
Today's most advanced agentic systems sit around stage 2-3: they choose strategies and gather some of their own experience
Nobody has a validated stage-5 example — an AI whose self-revised improvement process demonstrably beats the original in a controlled test
Use this taxonomy as a BS-detector: ask any 'self-improving AI' claim which stage it's actually demonstrating

questions.prompt: In this paper's taxonomy, what distinguishes stage 2 (Improvement-Strategy Autonomy) from stage 1 (Improvement-Execution Autonomy)?
options: Stage 2 systems run on more GPUs
Stage 2 systems decide WHAT to fix and HOW, not just execute a fix they're told to make
Stage 2 systems require no human oversight at all
Stage 2 is only about faster inference
questions.explanation: Stage 1 executes a specified fix; stage 2 adds diagnosis and strategy selection, while objectives and evaluation criteria are still externally set by humans.

questions.prompt: According to the paper, what have researchers found regarding stage 5 (Recursive Meta-Improvement)?
options: It has been fully achieved by several labs
Cases exist where an AI revised its own improvement method and the revision was adopted, but no case reliably showed it outperforming the original under a fair test
It's theoretically impossible
It only applies to robotics
questions.explanation: The paper is careful to separate 'a self-revision got used' from 'a self-revision was proven better' — the second, stricter bar hasn't been reliably cleared.

questions.prompt: Why does the paper note that different scenarios (software engineering vs. embodied robotics vs. scientific discovery) climb the RSI ladder at different speeds?
options: Because robotics hardware is more expensive
Because feedback loops differ in cost and simulatability — cheap, fast, simulatable feedback (like code tests) accelerates progress up the stages
Because software engineers write better papers
Speed doesn't actually differ across domains
questions.explanation: Domains where you can cheaply generate and verify experience (e.g., automated test suites) let systems climb toward experience-acquisition and adaptation autonomy faster than domains needing real-world, slow, expensive feedback.

posts.title: Chunking: Why Chunk Size Makes or Breaks RAG
posts.subtitle: The most underrated knob in retrieval — get it wrong and no embedding model can save you
posts.summary: Chunking splits documents into retrievable pieces before embedding them, and the strategy you pick (fixed-size, recursive, semantic, or sentence-window) directly controls what your RAG system can and can't answer. Too small loses context; too large drowns the signal — and no amount of reranking fixes a bad chunk boundary.

slides.title: Your retriever is only as good as its chunks
slides.body: Before a single embedding gets computed, someone has to decide where to cut a 40-page PDF into pieces. That decision — chunking — quietly caps the ceiling of every RAG system built on top of it.

slides.title: Why you can't just embed the whole document
slides.body: Embedding models compress text into a fixed-size vector. Cram in too much text and the vector becomes an average of everything — good at matching nothing specifically.
bullets: Most embedding models have an effective context limit (often 512-8k tokens) before quality degrades
A single vector for a 40-page doc can't distinguish 'refund policy' from 'shipping policy' — both blur into one point in vector space
Retrieval returns whole documents when it should return the three relevant sentences — wasting the LLM's context window on noise

slides.title: Four chunking strategies, in order of sophistication
bullets: Fixed-size: split every N tokens (e.g. 512) with some overlap (e.g. 50). Fast, simple, but cuts mid-sentence and mid-idea
Recursive character/token splitting: try to split on paragraph breaks first, then sentences, then words — falls back only when a chunk is still too big
Semantic chunking: embed consecutive sentences, and cut where the embedding similarity between neighbors drops sharply (a topic shift)
Sentence-window: index single sentences for precise matching, but retrieve a window of surrounding sentences for context — separates 'what matches' from 'what gets read'

slides.title: Chunk size is a tradeoff, not a free parameter

rows: Answer is technically retrieved but ungrounded/ambiguous
Relevant sentence buried in irrelevant text, gets outranked

slides.title: Worked example: a 20-page HR policy PDF
slides.body: A user asks: "How many sick days do I get in my first year?" The document has one sentence that answers this, buried in a 3-page 'Leave Policies' section.
bullets: Fixed 1000-token chunks: the answer sentence shares a chunk with vacation, parental leave, and bereavement policy — the embedding for that chunk is a blurry average, and it may not rank in the top-3 results
Recursive chunking on headers/paragraphs (~300 tokens): the sick-leave subsection becomes its own chunk, embedding is sharply about sick leave, retrieval nails it
Sentence-window: the single sentence with the number matches perfectly, and the system pulls in the paragraph around it so the LLM has enough context to phrase a full answer

slides.title: Pitfalls and when to skip fancy chunking
bullets: Semantic chunking costs an embedding call per sentence at index time — fine for a one-time corpus, expensive for constantly-updating data
Too much overlap between chunks (e.g. 50%) inflates your vector index size and slows retrieval for marginal recall gains
Chunking structured data (tables, code, FAQs) by raw token count often shreds a table mid-row — use format-aware splitters instead
If your corpus is already short, well-scoped documents (e.g. individual support tickets), skip chunking entirely — embed the whole thing

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: Chunking happens before embedding and reranking — get it wrong and later pipeline stages can't recover the lost signal
Start with recursive splitting at ~300-500 tokens with ~10-15% overlap; it's the reasonable default for most text
Use sentence-window or semantic chunking when precision matters more than pipeline simplicity (legal, medical, policy documents)
Always test chunking choices against real user questions, not just 'does it embed' — the failure mode is silent, not an error

questions.prompt: Why does embedding an entire 40-page document as one vector usually hurt retrieval?
options: Embedding models can't process long documents at all
The resulting vector becomes an average of everything in the document, making it hard to specifically match any single topic within it
It costs too much money to embed long text
Long documents can't be stored in a vector database
questions.explanation: A single vector has to represent the whole document, so distinct topics blur together into one point in vector space, hurting specific-topic matches.

questions.prompt: What does sentence-window chunking do differently from fixed-size chunking?
options: It indexes single sentences for precise matching, but retrieves a wider surrounding window for context — separating what matches from what gets read
It ignores sentence boundaries entirely
It only works for non-English text
It requires no embedding model
questions.explanation: By decoupling the match unit (a sentence) from the context unit (surrounding sentences), it gets precise retrieval without losing the context the LLM needs to answer well.

questions.prompt: According to the chunk-size tradeoff, what's the typical failure mode of chunks that are too large (1000+ tokens)?
options: The system crashes
The relevant sentence gets buried in irrelevant surrounding text, diluting the match signal enough that it may not rank highly
Large chunks always retrieve perfectly
Large chunks can't be embedded
questions.explanation: Large chunks dilute the embedding signal — the part of the chunk that actually answers the query is outweighed by unrelated surrounding text, which can push it out of the top results.

posts.title: Quantization: Shrinking LLMs Without Losing Their Minds
posts.subtitle: How rounding 16-bit weights to 4 bits turns a 4-GPU model into a laptop model
posts.summary: Quantization compresses an LLM's weights from 16-bit floats down to 8 or 4 bits, cutting memory and bandwidth roughly in half or in quarter. Methods like GPTQ and AWQ make this work by compensating for rounding error or protecting the small set of outlier channels that matter most, keeping quality nearly intact.

slides.title: Quantization: Shrinking LLMs Without Losing Their Minds
slides.body: A 70B model in full precision needs ~140GB of VRAM. Quantization gets it running on a single consumer GPU — by rounding, not retraining.

slides.title: Big Models Are Memory-Bound, Not Compute-Bound
slides.body: Serving an LLM one token at a time means the GPU spends most of its time waiting on weights to stream in from memory, not doing math. Fewer bytes per weight means faster generation, not just a smaller footprint.
bullets: FP16 stores each weight in 2 bytes: a 70B-parameter model needs ~140GB just for weights
A high-end consumer GPU has 24GB — that model doesn't fit without splitting across many GPUs
Autoregressive decoding re-reads the entire weight set for every single token, so memory bandwidth caps your tokens/sec
Cutting bytes-per-weight in half roughly doubles achievable throughput on the same hardware

slides.title: Round to Fewer Bits, Then Fix the Damage
slides.body: Naively rounding every weight to 4 bits tanks quality. The trick is compensating for that error instead of ignoring it.
bullets: Basic scheme: map a range of FP16 values to integers via a scale + zero-point, usually per small group of ~128 weights (not the whole tensor) to limit error

GPTQ quantizes one weight at a time and updates the *remaining unquantized* weights to absorb the rounding error, using second-order (Hessian) information — it processes a 175B model in a few GPU-hours
AWQ observes that ~1% of weight channels see much larger activation magnitudes than the rest; it keeps those salient channels at higher effective precision instead of treating every weight equally
Both are post-training: no retraining, no gradient updates — just a calibration pass over a few hundred sample sequences

slides.title: What You Give Up at Each Bit Width
slides.body: Typical published ranges for a ~70B-class model — exact numbers vary by model and calibration set.

rows: Usually edges out GPTQ at same width
Often too lossy without extra tricks

slides.title: Fitting a 13B Chat Model on an 8GB Laptop GPU
slides.body: Llama-2-13B at FP16 needs ~26GB — nowhere close to fitting. Quantize to 4-bit (llama.cpp's Q4_K_M-style format) and weights drop to roughly 6.5-7GB.
bullets: 6.5-7GB of weights plus a few GB for KV cache and activations comfortably fits an 8GB laptop GPU
This is exactly why GGUF (llama.cpp), GPTQ, and AWQ checkpoints of every popular open model get published within days of release
The same math is why a 70B model needs ~35-40GB at 4-bit — still too big for one 24GB card, which is why people reach for a 30-40B model instead at 4-bit, or accept 2 GPUs

slides.title: When Quantization Bites Back
slides.body: The failure modes are predictable once you know where the outliers live.
bullets: Below ~4 bits, naive per-tensor quantization degrades fast — those outlier activation channels AWQ protects get crushed, and math/reasoning-heavy tasks suffer more than fluent chit-chat
Quantizing the KV cache (not just weights) needs its own care — long, reasoning-heavy contexts are more sensitive to KV precision loss than short chats

Don't quantize a model you're about to fine-tune on new data — fine-tune in higher precision first (or use a method like QLoRA that's designed to fine-tune through a quantized base), then quantize for serving
Always re-run your own eval suite after quantizing — perplexity on a generic corpus can look fine while a narrow downstream task (tool-calling accuracy, code correctness) quietly regresses

slides.title: The Short Version
slides.body: Quantization trades a small, controllable amount of accuracy for a large, predictable amount of memory and speed.
bullets: Bytes-per-weight is the lever: FP16 → INT8 halves memory, → INT4 quarters it
GPTQ compensates for rounding error layer-by-layer; AWQ protects the small set of high-magnitude activation channels — pick AWQ first for speed, GPTQ when you need its tooling ecosystem
INT8 is close to a free lunch; INT4 costs a little quality for a lot of memory; below 4-bit gets risky without specialized methods
Always validate on your actual task after quantizing, not just generic perplexity

questions.prompt: Why is serving a large language model usually 'memory-bound' rather than 'compute-bound'?
options: GPUs cannot perform floating-point math fast enough for transformer layers
Autoregressive decoding re-reads the full set of weights from memory for every generated token, so memory bandwidth limits throughput
Quantized models require more matrix multiplications than full-precision ones
Attention layers require more VRAM than the model's weights
questions.explanation: Generating one token at a time means the GPU streams the entire weight set from memory on every step. That repeated memory traffic, not raw arithmetic, is usually the bottleneck — which is exactly why shrinking bytes-per-weight (quantization) speeds up generation, not just saves space.

questions.prompt: What does AWQ do differently from simply rounding every weight to the nearest 4-bit value?
options: It retrains the entire model from scratch at lower precision
It identifies the small set of weight channels tied to unusually large activation magnitudes and protects them from aggressive rounding
It only quantizes the attention layers and leaves the feed-forward layers in FP16
It increases the model's parameter count to compensate for lost precision
questions.explanation: AWQ's key observation is that a small fraction of channels (often under 1%) see much larger activations than the rest. Naively rounding those channels does disproportionate damage, so AWQ keeps them at effectively higher precision while quantizing the rest normally — no retraining needed.

questions.prompt: A 70B-parameter model needs roughly 140GB of VRAM at FP16. Roughly how much does it need at 4-bit quantization?
options: About 140GB — quantization only speeds up compute, not memory
About 70GB
About 35-40GB
About 5GB
questions.explanation: FP16 uses 2 bytes per weight; 4-bit uses roughly a quarter of that per weight (0.5 bytes), plus some overhead for scales and zero-points — so memory drops from ~140GB toward ~35-40GB. That's the difference between needing a multi-GPU server and fitting on one high-end consumer card.

posts.title: When Agents Slow Down: Tokens Stop Paying Off
posts.subtitle: A new Elo-per-token analysis shows agent test-time compute has a scaling inflection point — and parallel sessions beat one long one.
posts.summary: Researchers introduce Elo-per-token analysis to measure how LLM agent performance scales with token budget, using a Bradley-Terry model to compare best-so-far solutions across tasks with different scoring scales. Agents beat independent sampling early, then hit a scaling inflection point where marginal gains fall below baseline — after which splitting the same token budget across parallel sessions beats one long session.

slides.title: When Agents Slow Down: Tokens Stop Paying Off
slides.body: Give an agent 100M tokens and let it revise, branch, and backtrack — how do you even measure whether it's improving? A new paper builds a metric to answer that, and finds a hard scaling wall.

slides.title: Agents Don't Scale Like Pretraining
slides.body: Pretraining scaling laws plot loss against fixed compute. Agent test-time compute is different: the agent itself decides how to spend its budget — revise a draft, call a tool, explore an alternative, or just stop.
bullets: That adaptive behavior makes 'tokens spent' and 'quality gained' hard to compare across tasks with wildly different scoring scales
Naive fixes — average raw scores, or count task completions — either wash out signal or ignore how much better one solution is than another
The paper studies four general-purpose agents across four open-ended benchmarks, running sessions up to 100M tokens

slides.title: Elo-Per-Token: Turn Solutions Into a Ratings Ladder
slides.body: At every token budget, the method tracks the best solution the agent has found so far, then uses a Bradley-Terry model — the same math behind chess Elo — to convert head-to-head solution comparisons into a single rating.
bullets: Because Elo is relative (A beats B), it aggregates cleanly across tasks that score on completely different scales
Plotting Elo against tokens spent turns 'is the agent still improving' into a readable curve instead of a pile of incomparable numbers
The curve's shape is the point: early slope shows how efficiently tokens convert to quality, and where it bends shows when that efficiency runs out

slides.title: The Scaling Inflection Point
slides.body: Early on, an agent converts tokens into Elo faster than an 'independent sampling' baseline (drawing fresh, unrelated attempts). But marginal gains shrink as the session runs longer, and eventually the agent's rate falls below that baseline.
bullets: The token budget where marginal Elo gain drops to match the independent-sampling reference is the scaling inflection point
Past that point, the agent is mostly re-treading the same reasoning — more tokens buy little
This inflection point is exactly the signal you need to decide when to stop a session and start a fresh one instead

slides.title: Same 100M Tokens, Split Around the Inflection Point
slides.body: On the FrontierCS Polyomino Packing benchmark, the authors used the measured inflection point to size sessions, then compared that allocation against two naive alternatives for spending the same 100M-token budget.

headers: Elo gained by splitting at the inflection point instead
rows: Ten short parallel sessions (splitting too early)

slides.title: Humans Don't Hit the Same Wall — Yet
slides.body: The authors compared agents to the strongest human contestants on shared AtCoder Heuristic Contest tasks, where competitors keep refining a single solution over the whole contest window.
bullets: Top human contestants improve superlinearly over contest time — they get faster at getting better, not slower
Agents show the opposite curve: fast early gains, then diminishing and eventually sub-baseline returns
The gap implies real headroom: agents aren't yet using long thinking time the way strong humans do

slides.title: Where This Breaks Down
slides.body: Elo-per-token is a measurement tool, not a free lunch — it comes with real caveats before you act on it.
bullets: The inflection point is task- and model-specific; you have to measure it per agent/benchmark, not assume a universal budget
Bradley-Terry aggregation needs enough head-to-head comparisons to be stable — noisy on very small solution pools
Splitting into parallel sessions only pays off if sessions can be scored and compared; setups without a reliable evaluator can't apply this directly
Human superlinear improvement was measured on structured contest problems (AtCoder), which may not generalize to open-ended, hard-to-score tasks

slides.title: The Core Idea, in One Line
bullets: Elo-per-token turns 'is more test-time compute helping' into a comparable curve across tasks, via Bradley-Terry ratings on best-so-far solutions
Every agent studied hit a scaling inflection point: fast early gains, then sub-baseline marginal returns
Sizing sessions around that inflection point beat both a single long session (+264 Elo) and splitting too early into ten short ones (+355 Elo) on the tested benchmark

questions.prompt: Why do the authors convert agent solution quality into Elo ratings instead of comparing raw benchmark scores?
options: Elo ratings are cheaper to compute than raw scores
Raw scores from different tasks live on incomparable scales, but Elo's relative head-to-head comparisons via a Bradley-Terry model aggregate across them
Elo ratings eliminate the need for any baseline comparison
Benchmarks don't produce numeric scores at all
questions.explanation: Different tasks score in different units and ranges. Bradley-Terry-based Elo only needs 'is solution A better than solution B', which is comparable everywhere, so ratings can be aggregated across a whole benchmark suite.

questions.prompt: What defines the 'scaling inflection point' for an agent's test-time compute?
options: The token budget where the agent runs out of context window
The point where the agent calls its first tool
The token budget where marginal Elo gain per token drops to match an independent-sampling baseline
The moment the agent's temperature parameter changes
questions.explanation: Before the inflection point, the agent converts tokens into Elo faster than independent sampling. After it, marginal returns fall to (and eventually below) that baseline rate — a measurable signal for when a session has stopped paying off.

questions.prompt: On FrontierCS Polyomino Packing, what did sizing sessions around the measured inflection point demonstrate?
options: That a single long session always outperforms any parallel split
It beat both a single long session (+264 Elo) and splitting too early into ten short sessions (+355 Elo), for the same total 100M-token budget
That token budget has no effect on Elo once the model is fixed
That human contestants and agents scale identically
questions.explanation: Using the measured inflection point to size sessions beat both naive alternatives on the same total budget: one long session, and splitting too early into ten short ones. That's direct evidence the inflection point is a genuinely useful signal for allocating test-time compute, not just a descriptive curve.

posts.title: Reranking: The Second Pass RAG Pipelines Skip
posts.subtitle: Vector search finds candidates fast; a cross-encoder decides which ones actually matter.
posts.summary: Vector search retrieves candidates fast by comparing pre-computed embeddings, but similarity in embedding space isn't the same as relevance. Reranking adds a slower, more accurate second pass — a cross-encoder that reads the query and each candidate together — over a small shortlist, fixing ordering mistakes before anything reaches the LLM's context window.

slides.title: Reranking: The Second Pass RAG Pipelines Skip
slides.body: Your vector search returns 50 'similar' chunks in milliseconds. The problem: similar isn't the same as relevant, and the LLM only has room for the top handful. Reranking is the fix most RAG tutorials leave out.

slides.title: Bi-Encoders Trade Accuracy for Speed
slides.body: Vector search works by embedding the query and every document independently (a 'bi-encoder'), then ranking by cosine similarity — the two texts never actually see each other.
bullets: That independence is what makes it fast: documents are embedded once, offline, and the query only needs one embedding at query time
But it means the model can't reason about query and document jointly — a chunk that shares vocabulary can outrank one that actually answers the question
Top-k similarity search also has no concept of redundancy: five near-duplicate chunks can crowd out a genuinely different relevant one

slides.title: Cross-Encoders Read Query and Document Together
slides.body: A reranker feeds the query and a candidate document into the same model, concatenated, so attention layers can directly compare them token-by-token before producing one relevance score.
bullets: This joint attention is exactly what a bi-encoder can't do, and it's why cross-encoders consistently score relevance more accurately
The cost: no precomputing. Every query-document pair needs a fresh forward pass, so it doesn't scale to millions of documents directly
The fix is a two-stage pipeline: bi-encoder vector search narrows millions of documents to a shortlist (e.g. top 50-100), then the cross-encoder reranks only that shortlist

slides.title: Where Reranking Sits in the Pipeline
slides.body: Reranking is a filter stage, not a replacement for retrieval — it never sees documents vector search didn't already surface.
bullets: Stage 1 — Retrieve: bi-encoder + ANN index (e.g. HNSW) pulls top-50 to top-200 candidates by embedding similarity, in milliseconds even over millions of vectors
Stage 2 — Rerank: cross-encoder scores each of those candidates against the query and reorders them, in tens to low hundreds of milliseconds for that shortlist
Stage 3 — Truncate: only the reranked top 3-10 go into the LLM's context window, where every token has a real cost

slides.title: A Support Ticket That Vector Search Gets Wrong
slides.body: Query: 'Why does my API key stop working after I rotate it?' Vector search's top hit is a doc titled 'API Key Best Practices' that mentions rotation once in passing — high lexical/semantic overlap, low actual relevance.
bullets: Buried at rank 12 is a doc titled 'Cached Credentials and Rotation Downtime' that directly explains the caching layer causing the failure
A cross-encoder reading query and doc #12 together recognizes the causal match ('stop working after rotate' -> 'rotation downtime') that cosine similarity missed
After reranking, doc #12 moves into the top 3 that actually reach the LLM — the answer becomes reachable instead of buried past the context cutoff

slides.title: Bi-Encoder vs. Cross-Encoder: Know the Tradeoff
slides.body: Neither wins outright — that's why production RAG systems use both in sequence rather than picking one.

rows: Linear in candidates scored, no indexing
Can run over the whole corpus?

slides.title: When Reranking Isn't Worth It
slides.body: Reranking is a real latency and cost addition, not a free accuracy boost — apply it where the tradeoff actually pays off.
bullets: Tiny corpora (a few hundred chunks) rarely need it — retrieval alone is already accurate enough to skip the extra hop
Hard real-time paths (sub-100ms budgets) may not tolerate a cross-encoder pass on top of retrieval latency
If your bi-encoder's top-k is already narrow and consistently on-target, reranking adds cost without moving the needle
Rerankers inherit the biases of their training data just like any model — verify on your own query distribution, not just a public leaderboard

slides.title: The Core Idea, in One Line
bullets: Vector search is fast because it never lets query and document interact — that's also its main weakness
A cross-encoder reranker reads both together and reorders a small shortlist far more accurately, at a real latency cost
Use it as a second stage over dozens of candidates, not a replacement for retrieval over your whole corpus

questions.prompt: What's the fundamental architectural difference between a bi-encoder and a cross-encoder?
options: Bi-encoders are always larger models than cross-encoders
A bi-encoder embeds query and document independently; a cross-encoder processes them together so it can attend across both
Cross-encoders don't use neural networks
Bi-encoders can only handle short documents
questions.explanation: Bi-encoders compute separate embeddings for query and document (enabling fast precomputation and ANN search), while cross-encoders concatenate query and document into one forward pass so attention can directly compare them — more accurate, but not precomputable.

questions.prompt: Why do production RAG pipelines typically use vector search AND reranking together, rather than just one?
options: It's required by law in most jurisdictions
Cross-encoders can't produce embeddings at all
Vector search scales to the full corpus cheaply but is less accurate; reranking is accurate but too slow to run over millions of documents, so it narrows only a shortlist
Vector search is deprecated technology
questions.explanation: The two-stage design plays to each method's strength: ANN-indexed vector search cheaply narrows a huge corpus to dozens of candidates, and the cross-encoder spends its higher per-pair cost only on that small shortlist to get the ordering right.

questions.prompt: In which scenario is reranking LEAST likely to be worth adding to a RAG pipeline?
options: A support-ticket search over millions of documents where relevant answers are often several ranks below the top vector-search hit
A legal research tool where retrieval precision directly affects the answer quality
A tiny FAQ bot over a few hundred well-separated chunks with a strict sub-100ms latency budget
A codebase search where semantically similar but functionally different code often confuses vector similarity
questions.explanation: With a small, well-separated corpus, plain vector search is often already accurate enough, and a strict low-latency budget may not tolerate the extra cross-encoder pass — the cost of reranking isn't justified there the way it is for large or ambiguous corpora.
