posts.title: Constrained Decoding: Forcing LLMs to Output Valid JSON
posts.subtitle: Stop asking nicely in the prompt — make illegal tokens unsampleable.
posts.summary: Constrained decoding compiles a JSON Schema or grammar into an automaton and masks illegal tokens before sampling, so an LLM's output is guaranteed to parse and match your schema. It guarantees syntax, never semantics — hallucinated values still need downstream validation.

slides.title: Constrained Decoding: Forcing LLMs to Output Valid JSON
slides.body: Every agent that calls tools or fills a schema hits the same wall: LLMs sample freely, so they occasionally emit malformed JSON. Constrained decoding fixes this at the token level, not the prompt level.

slides.title: Prompting for JSON Only Gets You So Far
slides.body: Telling a model 'respond only in JSON' relies on the model choosing to comply — it's a suggestion, not a guarantee.
bullets: Common failures: trailing commas, unescaped quotes, wrong types (a string where a number belongs), stray prose before or after the JSON
Retrying on a parse failure burns latency and tokens, sometimes repeatedly
Failure rate climbs as schemas nest deeper or the model runs under time or token pressure

slides.title: Mask Out Every Token That Would Break the Grammar
slides.body: Constrained decoding compiles your JSON Schema (or any context-free grammar) into an automaton. At each decoding step it computes which tokens are legal given the current parse state, and sets the logits for everything else to -infinity before sampling.
bullets: The model still chooses freely among the tokens the grammar allows — it just can't emit an illegal one
The automaton is compiled once per schema, then walked incrementally: one state transition per generated token, not a full reparse
It layers under any decoding strategy — greedy, top-p, beam search — since it only edits the logit distribution before sampling runs

slides.title: From Regex to a Full JSON Schema: How the Automaton Is Built
slides.body: Libraries like Outlines and XGrammar turn a schema into a pushdown automaton over the tokenizer's actual vocabulary, then precompute which tokens are valid from each state.
bullets: Naive approach: try appending each candidate token and re-validate the whole string — far too slow to run every step
Fast approach: precompute a token-to-transition table offline, so the per-step cost is a vocabulary-sized bitmask, not a parse
Nested objects and arrays need a pushdown automaton, not a plain finite-state machine, to track unbounded nesting depth

slides.title: Three Ways to Get Structured Output
slides.body: The three common approaches trade guarantees for flexibility differently.

rows: Any JSON, not your specific shape
Yes — always parses and matches schema

slides.title: Extracting an Order From a Messy Customer Email
slides.body: Schema: { id: string, items: [{ sku: string, qty: integer }], total: number }. Mid-generation, right after "qty": 3, the automaton sits in a state that only allows , or } next.
bullets: If the model's top-ranked token were a rogue " (starting a new key without closing the array), the automaton masks it out entirely
The model resamples from what's left — , to add another item, or } to close the object — so it can't derail into invalid JSON
The email's typos and rambling don't matter; only the schema's shape has to hold

slides.title: What Constrained Decoding Doesn't Buy You
slides.body: It guarantees the output parses and matches your schema's shape — it says nothing about whether the values inside are correct.
bullets: A model can still hallucinate a confident but wrong total or invent a SKU that doesn't exist — syntax valid, content wrong
Very large or deeply recursive schemas (unbounded nested unions) can blow up automaton size and slow compilation
Skip libraries that re-validate token-by-token instead of precomputing the mask — that naive path carries a real latency tax
Combining it with speculative decoding takes extra care, since draft tokens must also satisfy the same mask

slides.title: The Core Idea, in One Line
bullets: Constrained decoding moves correctness from 'ask nicely in the prompt' to 'make illegal tokens unsampleable'
It guarantees syntax and schema shape, never semantic truth — still validate values downstream
Reach for it whenever a program, not a human, reads the model's output: tool calls, API payloads, structured extraction

questions.prompt: What does constrained (grammar-based) decoding actually guarantee about a model's output?
options: That the output will always be factually correct
That the output will always parse and match the given grammar or schema
That the model will run faster than unconstrained decoding
That the model no longer needs a system prompt
questions.explanation: Constrained decoding only restricts which tokens are legal at each step, so it guarantees syntactic validity, not factual correctness. A model can still confidently fill in a wrong number inside a perfectly valid JSON object.

questions.prompt: Mechanically, how does constrained decoding stop a model from emitting an invalid token?
options: It fine-tunes the model on valid examples before generation starts
It re-runs the whole generation from scratch whenever a token turns out invalid
It masks the logits of any token that would violate the grammar's current state, before sampling
It asks a second LLM to fix the output after generation finishes
questions.explanation: The automaton tracks a parse state per generated token and computes, ahead of sampling, which vocabulary tokens are legal transitions from that state. Illegal tokens get their logits set to -infinity so they can never be sampled — no retry or post-hoc fixup needed.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a genuine limitation of constrained decoding?
options: It can't be combined with top-p or beam search
Deeply recursive or very large schemas can blow up automaton size and slow compilation
It only works with one specific model provider
It requires retraining the base model
questions.explanation: Constrained decoding sits on top of any sampling strategy and needs no retraining — but a pushdown automaton for a large or deeply recursive schema can have many states, making compilation and mask computation slower and more memory-heavy.

posts.title: FlashAttention: Attention Is Memory-Bound, Not Compute-Bound
posts.subtitle: The kernel trick that made long-context training fit on a single GPU
posts.summary: Standard attention is slow not because of FLOPs but because it repeatedly reads and writes a full N×N score matrix to slow GPU memory. FlashAttention fuses the whole operation into tiles that stay in fast on-chip SRAM, computing the exact same softmax attention output in O(N) memory instead of O(N²) — no approximation, just smarter I/O.

slides.title: The Bottleneck Was Never the Math
slides.body: GPUs can do far more floating-point operations per second than they can move bytes between memory tiers. Standard attention ignores that asymmetry — FlashAttention is built around it.

slides.title: Standard Attention Is Memory-Bound, Not FLOP-Bound
slides.body: Computing softmax(QKᵀ)V naively means materializing the full N×N score matrix in GPU high-bandwidth memory (HBM), then reading it back for softmax, then again for the V multiply.
bullets: GPU compute (TFLOPs) has scaled much faster than HBM bandwidth over the last decade
Every intermediate N×N matrix gets written to and re-read from slow HBM, not the fast on-chip SRAM
Result: attention spends most of its wall-clock time waiting on memory transfers, while the GPU's compute cores sit idle

slides.title: Tile the Computation, Never Materialize the Full Matrix
slides.body: FlashAttention splits Q, K, and V into small blocks sized to fit in SRAM, then fuses the matmul, softmax, and second matmul into a single kernel per tile.
bullets: Blocks of Q, K, V are loaded into SRAM once and reused across the tile's computation
An 'online softmax' running-max/running-sum trick lets each tile update the correct normalized output incrementally, without ever seeing the full row of scores at once
The final output is mathematically IDENTICAL to standard softmax attention — this is an exact algorithm, not an approximation like sparse or linear attention

slides.title: The Backward Pass Trades Compute for Memory
slides.body: Standard backprop through attention stores the N×N matrix from the forward pass to reuse in gradients. FlashAttention instead throws it away and recomputes it.
bullets: Storing O(N²) activations for backward would defeat the whole point of tiling
Instead, the forward pass keeps only the small per-row softmax statistics (max and sum) needed to recompute scores on demand
Recomputation adds extra FLOPs in the backward pass — but since compute is cheap relative to HBM I/O on modern GPUs, it's still a net speedup

slides.title: Standard vs. Tiled Attention

rows: Exact — bit-identical up to floating-point rounding
Recomputes scores from Q/K/V on the fly
Same O(N²) — this optimizes I/O, not arithmetic complexity

slides.title: Why 16K Context Used to Just Not Fit
slides.body: The memory math makes the problem concrete: a single attention score matrix at long context length is enormous before you even get to storing activations for backprop.
bullets: At sequence length N = 16,384, one N×N score matrix in fp16 is 16384² × 2 bytes ≈ 512 MB — for ONE attention head, in ONE layer, for ONE example
Multiply that by dozens of layers and heads per batch item, and standard attention runs out of memory long before the rest of the model even loads
FlashAttention never allocates that matrix at all, so the same GPU that couldn't fit a 2K-token standard-attention layer can train at 16K+ tokens

slides.title: When It Doesn't Help — or Doesn't Apply
slides.body: FlashAttention is a systems-level win, not a free lunch in every setting.
bullets: It needs a custom fused kernel for the specific GPU architecture — support lags on new hardware or non-NVIDIA backends
For very short sequences, the N×N matrix already fits comfortably in cache; tiling overhead can erase the benefit
It doesn't reduce the underlying O(N²) FLOPs of attention — for extreme context lengths you still need complementary tricks (sliding window, sparse attention) to cut compute, not just memory traffic
Because it changes floating-point accumulation order, results can differ from naive attention in the last few bits of precision — rarely an issue, but not bit-for-bit identical in practice

slides.title: The Core Idea, Distilled
slides.body: Know the bottleneck before you optimize the math.
bullets: Attention's real cost on GPUs is memory movement, not floating-point math
Tiling + fused kernels + online softmax = exact attention in linear memory
Recomputing in the backward pass is a deliberate compute-for-memory trade, not an oversight
It's now the default attention implementation behind most production LLM training and serving stacks

questions.prompt: What is the primary bottleneck FlashAttention is designed to fix?
options: The raw number of floating-point operations (FLOPs) attention requires
Repeated reads/writes of the full N×N attention matrix to slow GPU HBM
Network bandwidth between multiple GPUs
Python interpreter overhead in the training loop
questions.explanation: GPUs have far more compute throughput than memory bandwidth. Standard attention is memory-bound because it repeatedly shuttles the full N×N score matrix between fast on-chip SRAM and slow HBM — FlashAttention targets that I/O pattern, not the arithmetic itself.

questions.prompt: How does FlashAttention avoid ever storing the complete N×N attention matrix?
options: It approximates attention using a fixed sparse pattern
It processes Q/K/V in small SRAM-sized tiles and uses an online (running) softmax to combine partial results correctly
It drops the softmax step entirely
It quantizes all activations to int8 before computing attention
questions.explanation: The core trick is tiling combined with an online softmax: each tile updates a running max and running sum so the final normalized output is exactly correct, without ever holding a full row of scores in memory at once.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly describes a genuine tradeoff of FlashAttention?
options: It reduces attention's O(N²) FLOP count to O(N)
It recomputes attention scores during the backward pass instead of storing them, trading extra compute for far less memory use
It only runs on CPUs, not GPUs
It produces an approximate result, like sparse or linear attention
questions.explanation: FlashAttention is an exact algorithm — it still does O(N²) FLOPs. What it changes is memory strategy: rather than storing the N×N matrix for backprop, it recomputes it from Q/K/V on demand, which is a good trade because compute is cheap relative to HBM bandwidth on modern GPUs.

posts.title: FreeToken: Running a 753B Model on One Gaming GPU
posts.subtitle: Berkeley and MIT researchers turn scarce PCIe bandwidth into a live scheduling signal so frontier MoE models fit on a single consumer GPU.
posts.summary: FreeToken is an edge-native serving engine that treats a single gaming PC as an elastic inference platform for huge Mixture-of-Experts models. By making bandwidth-adaptive execution, expert caching, and elastic VRAM management the center of the design instead of an afterthought, it lets a 753B-parameter model run on one workstation GPU — though independent testers note the speedup isn't uniform across every setup.

slides.title: 753 Billion Parameters. One Gaming GPU.
slides.body: A team from UC Berkeley and MIT — including Ion Stoica, Matei Zaharia, and Song Han — built an inference engine that fits frontier-scale Mixture-of-Experts models onto hardware you can buy at a electronics store.

slides.title: MoE Models Grew Faster Than Consumer VRAM
slides.body: Modern open MoE models like GLM-5.2 (753B total params) or DeepSeek-V4-Flash (284B) only activate a fraction of their weights per token, but the FULL weight set still has to live somewhere reachable.
bullets: A gaming GPU tops out around 16-24GB VRAM; a 753B MoE model in low precision still needs hundreds of GB of storage
Naive fixes swap experts from CPU RAM or SSD on demand, but agent workloads jump between prefill-heavy and decode-heavy patterns unpredictably
Static CPU/GPU splits (pick some layers for GPU, rest for CPU) waste VRAM when the split doesn't match the current workload

slides.title: Bandwidth Becomes a Scheduling Signal, Not a Wall
slides.body: Instead of a fixed memory layout, FreeToken continuously decides which experts stay resident in VRAM versus stream from CPU RAM or NVMe, based on real-time PCIe/NVMe bandwidth availability.
bullets: Double-buffered prefill streaming overlaps expert loading with compute so the GPU is rarely stalled waiting on a weight transfer
A custom FTW (fast weight) format is designed for quick partial loads instead of generic checkpoint formats
A global LRU cache keeps the most bandwidth-expensive-to-reload experts resident across requests, not just within one

slides.title: Semantic Caching Keeps Agent State Alive
slides.body: Agentic workloads (coding assistants, tool-using agents) repeatedly revisit and edit earlier context, so FreeToken caches more than raw tokens.
bullets: Anchor checkpoints capture recurrent state and KV cache so an edited prompt can reuse unaffected prefix work instead of recomputing it
Elastic memory management dynamically reallocates VRAM between the expert cache and the KV cache without restarting the serving engine
This targets the actual usage pattern of coding agents — small edits to a large shared context — rather than one-shot batch inference

slides.title: The Headline Numbers
slides.body: Reported throughput on MoE models across three hardware tiers, per the authors' benchmarks.
bullets: Time-to-first-token: under 44s for FreeToken vs 232s for llama.cpp vs 946s for KTransformers in the authors' tests
Independent testers on an RTX 5060 8GB report llama.cpp already reaching 34.9 tok/s on Qwen3.6-35B, close to FreeToken's 39.3 tok/s — the gap narrows outside the authors' own benchmarks

slides.title: A Coding Agent on a Desktop, Not a Rack
slides.body: A developer runs a 284B-parameter DeepSeek-V4-Flash as a local coding agent on a single 32GB workstation GPU using FreeToken's Anthropic/OpenAI-compatible API.
bullets: The agent edits the same 20k-token file repeatedly — anchor checkpoints let each edit reuse the unaffected KV cache instead of recomputing the whole prefix
Bandwidth-adaptive execution keeps the frequently-used experts (e.g. code-related routing paths) resident in VRAM across the session
No cloud API calls, no per-token billing, and the model never leaves the machine

slides.title: It's a Workload Match, Not a Universal Speedup
slides.body: FreeToken's gains are real but conditional — the comparisons that make headlines aren't guaranteed on every setup.
bullets: Its advantage comes from optimizing for bursty, agentic access patterns; for steady batch decoding, gains over llama.cpp shrink significantly
You still need enough combined VRAM + system RAM to hold the active working set — it doesn't shrink the model, it schedules around scarce bandwidth
Ollama and llama.cpp optimize for GGUF quantization and simple layer offload; vLLM/SGLang target datacenter throughput — FreeToken competes in a specific middle niche (consumer MoE serving)

slides.title: What to Remember
bullets: FreeToken makes bandwidth — not VRAM capacity alone — the thing you schedule around when serving MoE models on consumer hardware
Bandwidth-adaptive execution + a global expert LRU cache + a fast weight format are the three load-bearing ideas
Semantic-aware caching (anchor checkpoints) is what makes it good for agents specifically, not just raw throughput
Treat the marketed multipliers skeptically — independent benchmarks on some hardware show a smaller gap versus llama.cpp than the launch numbers imply

questions.prompt: What does FreeToken treat as the primary constraint to schedule around, rather than VRAM capacity alone?
options: GPU clock speed
Available memory bandwidth (PCIe/NVMe)
Number of CPU cores
Network latency to the cloud
questions.explanation: FreeToken's core idea is bandwidth-adaptive execution: it decides what to keep resident in VRAM versus stream from CPU/SSD based on real-time bandwidth availability, turning a fixed bottleneck into a scheduling signal.

questions.prompt: Why do anchor checkpoints matter specifically for agentic coding workloads?
options: They compress the model weights permanently
They let edits to a large shared context reuse unaffected prefix computation instead of recomputing it
They increase the model's parameter count
They replace the need for a draft model
questions.explanation: Agents repeatedly revisit and lightly edit large contexts. Anchor checkpoints cache recurrent/KV state so an edit only recomputes what actually changed, which matters far more for agentic loops than for one-shot generation.

questions.prompt: What's the fair caveat about FreeToken's headline speedup numbers?
options: They only work on Apple Silicon
They require a cloud connection to function
They come from the authors' own benchmarks; independent testers on some hardware saw a smaller gap vs. llama.cpp
They only apply to dense (non-MoE) models
questions.explanation: Like most systems papers, the strongest numbers come from the authors' chosen configurations. Independent testing (e.g., on an RTX 5060 8GB) found llama.cpp already competitive on some models, so the real-world advantage varies by hardware and workload.

bullets: Apple originally previewed the new Siri at WWDC and slipped the release multiple times

rows: Complex Siri / photo editing / Image Playground

posts.title: Speculative Decoding: Draft Fast, Verify in Parallel
posts.subtitle: A cheap draft model guesses several tokens ahead; the big model checks them all in one pass — turning sequential decoding into parallel verification, with zero change to the output.
posts.summary: Speculative decoding uses a small draft model to guess several tokens ahead, then lets the large target model verify all of them in a single parallel forward pass — accepting the ones that match and discarding the rest via exact rejection sampling. The result is 2-5x faster generation with mathematically identical output, now standard in vLLM, SGLang, and TensorRT-LLM.

slides.title: Why Wait One Token at a Time?
slides.body: Autoregressive decoding generates a token, feeds it back in, and generates the next — strictly sequential. Speculative decoding breaks that bottleneck without changing a single output token.

slides.title: Decoding Is Memory-Bound, Not Compute-Bound
slides.body: Each decode step reads the model's entire weight set from GPU memory to produce just one token, so the GPU's compute sits mostly idle waiting on memory bandwidth.
bullets: A modern GPU can do far more FLOPs per second than a batch-size-1 decode step actually uses
This is why decoding throughput is often far below what the GPU's raw compute could theoretically support
Simply generating more tokens per forward pass would use that idle compute — the question is how to do it without guessing wrong

slides.title: Draft, Then Verify in One Shot
slides.body: A small, fast draft model autoregressively proposes γ tokens ahead (commonly 4-6). The large target model then evaluates all γ+1 candidate positions in a single parallel forward pass — the same cost as generating just one token normally, since verification is compute-bound, not sequential.
bullets: Rejection sampling accepts each drafted token only if it's consistent with the target model's exact probability distribution
The moment a token is rejected, the process resamples correctly from the target's distribution at that position and discards everything after
Output distribution is provably identical to standard decoding — this is lossless acceleration, not approximation

slides.title: EAGLE: Drafting From the Target's Own Features
slides.body: Instead of a fully separate small language model, the EAGLE family drafts using the target model's own hidden states plus a lightweight prediction head.
bullets: Feature-level drafting aligns more closely with the target model's actual distribution, raising the acceptance rate
P-EAGLE (contributed to vLLM by AWS in early 2026) drafts all K candidate tokens in one parallel pass instead of sequentially, cutting drafting overhead further
On coding benchmarks, P-EAGLE reaches a 20-30% improvement over EAGLE-3 alone

slides.title: Speedup Tracks the Acceptance Rate
slides.body: The higher the fraction of drafted tokens the target model accepts (α), the bigger the win — and how predictable the text is drives α.

slides.title: A Support Chatbot Serving More Users, Same Hardware
slides.body: A customer-support bot runs Llama-3.3-70B with an EAGLE-3 draft head in front of vLLM.
bullets: Median response latency drops roughly in proportion to the achieved speedup, because more tokens land per GPU forward pass
With the same latency budget per user, one GPU can now serve substantially more concurrent conversations
No retraining of the 70B model and no change to its outputs — the draft head is the only new component

slides.title: When It Doesn't Help
bullets: A poorly-aligned or too-large draft model can cost more compute than it saves — the draft has to be genuinely cheap relative to the target
High-entropy, creative generation (brainstorming, poetry) has a lower natural acceptance rate than boilerplate or code, shrinking the speedup
It adds serving complexity: a second model to load, keep in sync with the target, and monitor
It doesn't shrink time-to-first-token — prefill is still one pass; the win is entirely in the decode phase
At very large batch sizes, the server may already be compute-bound, at which point spare compute for drafting/verifying shrinks and gains diminish

slides.title: What to Remember
bullets: Speculative decoding exploits idle GPU compute during memory-bound decode steps by verifying multiple guessed tokens in one pass
It's mathematically lossless: rejection sampling guarantees the exact same output distribution as normal decoding
Speedup is driven by the draft's acceptance rate — the closer the small model tracks the big one, the bigger the win
It's now standard production infrastructure in vLLM, SGLang, and TensorRT-LLM — not a research curiosity

questions.prompt: Why is verifying γ drafted tokens roughly as expensive as generating just one token normally?
options: Because the draft model does all the work
Because verification is a single parallel forward pass over the γ+1 positions, which is compute-bound rather than memory-bound like sequential decoding
Because γ is always set to 1
Because the target model skips reading its own weights during verification
questions.explanation: Normal decoding is memory-bandwidth-bound because each step only produces one token per full weight read. Verifying several candidate positions at once is a batched, compute-bound operation that costs about the same as one memory-bound step, which is exactly the idle capacity speculative decoding exploits.

questions.prompt: What guarantees that speculative decoding doesn't change the model's output distribution?
options: The draft model is trained to be identical to the target model
Rejection sampling accepts drafted tokens only when consistent with the target's exact probabilities, and correctly resamples at the first mismatch
The target model is run twice and the results are averaged
Output tokens are rounded to the nearest valid vocabulary entry
questions.explanation: The rejection sampling step is what makes this lossless: a token is kept only if it matches what the target model's own distribution would have produced, and any rejection point correctly resamples from the target's distribution rather than the draft's.

questions.prompt: In which scenario would speculative decoding likely deliver the SMALLEST speedup?
options: Generating boilerplate code with a coding assistant
Answering a highly predictable, templated support query
Freeform creative writing with high output entropy
Autocompleting a common phrase
questions.explanation: Speedup tracks the draft's acceptance rate, and acceptance rate tracks how predictable the text is. High-entropy creative generation is harder for a small draft model to predict correctly, so fewer drafted tokens get accepted and the speedup shrinks.

posts.title: MLA: Compressing the KV Cache Without Losing Quality
posts.subtitle: DeepSeek's trick for making long-context serving cheap: cache a compressed latent, not full-size keys and values.
posts.summary: Multi-Head Latent Attention (MLA), introduced in DeepSeek-V2, shrinks the KV cache by storing a single compressed latent vector per token instead of full-size keys and values per head, then reconstructing them on the fly — cutting serving memory dramatically while matching or beating standard attention's quality.

slides.title: MLA: Compressing the KV Cache Without Losing Quality
slides.body: Multi-Head Latent Attention (MLA) is the attention variant behind DeepSeek-V2 and V3's cheap long-context serving. It's a different answer to the KV cache problem than the more familiar GQA.

slides.title: The KV cache is what actually limits your context window
slides.body: During inference, standard Multi-Head Attention (MHA) caches a full-size key and value vector per attention head, per token, so every token you generate keeps growing that cache. It's not the model weights that blow your GPU memory at long context — it's this cache.
bullets: Cache size scales with context length × batch size × number of heads — all three compound
Grouped-Query Attention (GQA) fixes this by sharing K/V across groups of heads, but that sharing reduces the model's expressivity
Bigger caches mean fewer concurrent users you can serve per GPU, directly setting your API's cost per token

slides.title: Cache a compressed latent, reconstruct it just-in-time
slides.body: MLA takes a different approach from GQA: instead of sharing K/V across heads, it projects K and V down into one small low-rank latent vector per token via a learned down-projection matrix. Only that latent gets cached. At attention time, learned up-projection matrices expand it back into full per-head keys and values.
bullets: The cache stores one compact latent per token, not one K/V pair per head
Up/down-projection matrices are learned during pretraining, not bolted on afterward
DeepSeek-V2's report shows MLA needs only a small fraction of standard MHA's cache size — and still outperforms MHA on quality

slides.title: The catch: RoPE doesn't compress cleanly
slides.body: Rotary position embeddings (RoPE) rotate query/key vectors based on position, and that rotation doesn't commute with MLA's low-rank compression. DeepSeek's fix is 'decoupled RoPE': split each key into a compressed content part (handled by MLA) and a small separate part that carries positional info directly, uncompressed.
bullets: Without this split, compressing then rotating (or rotating then compressing) would corrupt position information
The decoupled RoPE part is small relative to the compressed content part, so it adds little cache overhead
This detail is why MLA can't be bolted onto a RoPE model by just adding a projection layer — it needs architecture-level support

slides.title: MLA vs. GQA vs. standard MHA
slides.body: Different points on the same tradeoff: how much of standard MHA's KV cache do you keep, and what does that cost in quality?

rows: shared across head groups (varies by group size)
single-digit % of MHA on large MoE models
matches or exceeds MHA per DeepSeek's report

slides.title: Why this is why DeepSeek serves long context cheaply
slides.body: Picture a 128K-token chat session served on a fixed GPU budget. With standard MHA, the KV cache for that one session already eats a large chunk of memory, so you can host relatively few such sessions concurrently. Compress each token's cache entry to a small latent, and the same GPU can hold far more concurrent long-context sessions.
bullets: This is a direct lever on cost-per-token at serving time, not just a training-time trick
It's a structural reason DeepSeek's API pricing has undercut comparable-quality Western models
The saving compounds with batch size — more concurrent users, not just longer context per user

slides.title: When MLA is (and isn't) the right call
slides.body: MLA isn't a free lunch — it trades implementation and training complexity for serving efficiency.
bullets: Worth it when: you're serving long contexts at high concurrency and inference cost dominates (exactly DeepSeek's situation)
Adds real complexity: extra up/down-projection matrices, decoupled RoPE handling — harder to implement correctly than plain MHA or GQA
Not a drop-in retrofit: models are typically pretrained with MLA from the start rather than converted after the fact
If your bottleneck is compute (FLOPs) rather than memory, or your contexts are short, GQA's simplicity may be the better tradeoff

questions.prompt: What does MLA actually store in the KV cache, instead of full-size keys and values per head?
options: Nothing — it recomputes attention from scratch every step
A single compressed low-rank latent vector per token, expanded back to full size only when needed
A quantized (lower-precision) copy of the full K/V pairs
Only the value vectors, discarding all keys
questions.explanation: MLA down-projects K and V into one small latent vector per token for caching, then up-projects it back to full per-head K/V at attention time — that's where the memory savings come from.

questions.prompt: Why does MLA need 'decoupled RoPE' instead of applying rotary position embeddings normally?
options: RoPE is too slow to compute at inference time
RoPE's rotation doesn't commute with MLA's low-rank compression, so position info would be corrupted without a separate uncompressed path
Decoupled RoPE makes the model support longer context than the original RoPE
It's purely a licensing workaround, not a technical requirement
questions.explanation: Compressing a vector and then rotating it (or vice versa) doesn't give the same result as rotating first, since the operations don't commute — so DeepSeek splits keys into a compressed content part and a small uncompressed part that carries position directly.

questions.prompt: How does MLA's tradeoff differ from GQA's?
options: GQA shares K/V heads across groups to shrink cache size, at some cost to expressivity; MLA compresses into a latent and reconstructs it, aiming to shrink cache without that expressivity loss
They are two names for the exact same mechanism
GQA is only usable in vision models, MLA only in language models
MLA increases cache size to improve quality, the opposite of GQA's goal
questions.explanation: GQA reduces cache by having multiple query heads share fewer K/V heads. MLA takes a different path — compress-then-reconstruct via low-rank projections — which DeepSeek's report shows can shrink the cache even further while matching or beating standard MHA quality.

posts.title: Vidu S2: Real-Time Video You Can Edit Mid-Stream
posts.subtitle: One model generates an interactive avatar live; another rewrites a video stream while it plays.
posts.summary: Vidu S2, from Shengshu AI, pairs a real-time interactive avatar model with a real-time video-stream editor, both running fast enough for human-in-the-loop interaction. It beats strong offline and streaming baselines on editing quality while exploring real-time spatial (3D-aware) video generation.

slides.title: Vidu S2: Real-Time Video You Can Edit Mid-Stream
slides.body: Published September 15, 2026 by Shengshu AI (makers of the Vidu video models). Two systems, one paper: a live digital avatar you can direct as it generates, and a live editor that rewrites an existing video stream frame by frame.

slides.title: Video models are good, but not interactive
slides.body: Most video generation runs offline: you submit a prompt, wait seconds to minutes, and get a fixed clip back. That's fine for a one-shot render — useless for a live avatar, a game character, or a video call filter that has to react to you in the moment.
bullets: Offline generation can't take new instructions once it starts rendering
Editing an existing video stream (swap the outfit, change the background) normally means re-rendering the whole clip
Prior 'real-time' systems (the paper's own predecessor, Vidu S1) proved live generation was possible but not live editing

slides.title: Two specialized real-time models, one shared engine
slides.body: Vidu S2 splits the problem into generation and editing, but both lean on the same real-time recipe: Self-Replay Forcing to keep autoregressive generation stable frame after frame, plus hybrid attention, quantization, kernel fusion, and multi-GPU scheduling to hit interactive latency.
bullets: Vidu S2-Avatar: generates an interactive digital character from scratch, live
Vidu S2-Editing: takes an existing video stream and edits it in real time
Self-Replay Forcing stops the usual autoregressive-video failure mode where small errors compound into drift over long generations

slides.title: Avatar: swap the reference mid-generation
slides.body: Vidu S2-Avatar generates 720p video at 25–42 FPS and accepts a 'dynamic reference' — a driving image or instruction — that can change at any moment while it's running, not just at the start.
bullets: Example: start with a static character reference, then mid-stream tell it to 'start dancing' — it follows without restarting
Reference-following is explicitly stronger than Vidu S1's, per the paper
Targets use cases like live digital hosts and interactive characters, not pre-rendered cutscenes

slides.title: Editing: a live filter driven by text, not a fixed effect
slides.body: Vidu S2-Editing operates on a running video stream and supports style rendering, clothing replacement, character replacement, and background replacement — all while the stream keeps playing, not as a batch re-render.
bullets: Think of it as a semantic camera filter: 'change the background to a beach' applied live
The paper also studies real-time spatial (3D-aware) video generation as an extension of both models
This is the harder of the two problems: it has to stay temporally consistent with content it didn't generate

slides.title: Beats both offline and streaming baselines
slides.body: On the paper's editing benchmarks, Vidu S2-Editing scores higher than the strongest offline editor and the strongest prior streaming editor — despite running in real time, which is usually the harder constraint to satisfy.

slides.title: Why this matters beyond video demos
slides.body: Real-time, steerable generation is the same problem agentic AI keeps running into elsewhere: can the model take new information mid-task instead of only at the start? Vidu S2 is a concrete answer for video.
bullets: Real-time editing needs both speed (quantization, kernel fusion, multi-GPU scheduling) AND stability (Self-Replay Forcing) — one without the other fails
Splitting 'generate' and 'edit' into separate specialized models beat trying to do both with one system
Interactive video is still 720p and short-horizon — not a replacement for offline cinematic generation, just a different product category
Try the live demo at vidu.com/vidu-stream to see the latency tradeoffs firsthand

questions.prompt: What problem does 'Self-Replay Forcing' solve in Vidu S2?
options: It compresses the video file size for streaming
It keeps long autoregressive video generation stable instead of drifting/degrading over time
It replaces the need for a GPU during inference
It translates text prompts into a different language
questions.explanation: Autoregressive video generation tends to accumulate small errors frame after frame until quality collapses. Self-Replay Forcing is the training technique Vidu S2 uses to keep generation stable over long, live sessions.

questions.prompt: What's the key difference between Vidu S2-Avatar and Vidu S2-Editing?
options: Avatar only works offline, Editing only works in real time
Avatar generates a new interactive character from scratch; Editing modifies an existing live video stream
They are the same model with different names
Avatar produces audio, Editing produces video
questions.explanation: Avatar is a generation model (it creates the character/video live), while Editing takes an already-running video stream and rewrites it — style, clothing, character, or background — in real time.

questions.prompt: On the paper's editing benchmarks, how did Vidu S2-Editing compare to the strongest baselines?
options: It scored lower than both the offline and streaming baselines but was much faster
It tied with offline baselines and lost to streaming baselines
It outscored both the strongest offline baseline (Bernini-R 14B) and the strongest streaming baseline (Decart-Lucy2.5)
It was not compared to any baselines
questions.explanation: Vidu S2-Editing posted a joint overall score of 4.26 versus 3.92 for the offline baseline Bernini-R 14B, and 3.78 versus 3.71 for the streaming baseline Decart-Lucy2.5 on RefVIE — beating both while running in real time.

posts.title: SAS: Sparse Attention That Ranks Its Own Context
posts.subtitle: An end-to-end trained gate beats distillation-based sparse attention at tight budgets
posts.summary: SAS (Simple Attention Sparsification) is a Tencent Hunyuan paper trending on Hugging Face's Daily Papers that attaches continuous, learnable gates to blocks of context and lets the language-modeling loss itself optimize which blocks each query attends to — instead of distilling a separate selector from the original model's dense attention. Across reasoning, long-context, and agentic tasks it beats prior trainable sparse-attention baselines, with the widest margins at the tightest attention budgets.

slides.title: Full Attention Doesn't Scale — So Models Fake It
slides.body: Transformer attention costs grow quadratically with context length. Once contexts hit hundreds of thousands of tokens, computing full attention over every token pair becomes the dominant cost. SAS is a new post-training method for deciding, cheaply and per-query, which slice of that context is actually worth attending to.
bullets: Trending #1 on Hugging Face Daily Papers this week
From Tencent Hunyuan — arXiv 2609.13141
Open code + weights released alongside the paper

slides.title: Distillation-Based Selectors Can't Beat Their Teacher
slides.body: Most trainable sparse-attention methods train a lightweight selector to imitate the pattern of the original model's dense attention. That's a ceiling, not a target: the selector is only ever learning to copy scores that were never optimized for the sparsification task in the first place.
bullets: Selector is trained to match dense-attention scores, not to minimize the real language-modeling loss
Any mismatch between 'looks like dense attention' and 'is actually the useful context' never gets corrected
Performance quietly caps out well below what the architecture could support

slides.title: Continuous Gates Make Selection Differentiable
slides.body: SAS attaches a continuous, learnable gate to each candidate context block. Because the gate is continuous (not a hard discrete pick), gradients from the ordinary language-modeling loss flow straight through it — so the model learns which blocks matter for the actual downstream objective, with no separate distillation target and no dense-attention teacher required at training time.
bullets: Gates are optimized end-to-end with the LM loss, not by imitation
No frozen dense-attention teacher needed during training
Context ranking becomes a first-class, directly-optimized part of the model

slides.title: The Unit of Selection Is Blocks, Not Tokens
slides.body: SAS scores and selects 'context units' — contiguous blocks of tokens — rather than individual tokens. Operating at block granularity keeps the selection budget-controllable and hardware-friendly (blocks map cleanly onto the tiled matmuls GPUs already do for attention), while still letting the per-query gate scores decide which blocks survive.
bullets: Query-dependent: different queries can keep different blocks
Block granularity trades a little precision for big efficiency wins on real hardware
The attention budget (how many blocks to keep) is a tunable knob, not fixed at train time

slides.title: The Gap Widens as the Budget Shrinks
slides.body: The paper reports that SAS consistently outperforms trainable sparse-attention baselines across attention budgets — and that the advantage is largest precisely when the budget is tightest, i.e. when the model can only keep a small fraction of the context.

rows: Matches dense baseline, no teacher needed
Accuracy drops sharply — capped by teacher quality
Reported largest relative gains over baselines

slides.title: A 200-Page Contract, One Buried Clause
slides.body: Say a model is asked a question that hinges on a single indemnification clause on page 80 of a 200-page contract loaded into a long context window. A distillation-based selector picks blocks that merely 'look important' to a frozen dense-attention pattern — which may or may not include page 80. SAS's gates were trained against the actual task loss, so they're pushed to keep whatever blocks the model needs to answer correctly, including a narrow, unusual clause a generic importance heuristic would miss.
bullets: Selection is task-driven, not just 'attention-pattern-shaped'
Matters most exactly when the needle is easy to miss

slides.title: When Learned Sparsity Isn't the Right Call
slides.body: SAS is a post-training method: it needs a fine-tuning phase on the target model, unlike training-free heuristics (fixed local+global windows, streaming attention) that need zero extra training. That extra step buys better accuracy at aggressive sparsity, at the cost of engineering complexity and a training run you have to redo if you change the deployment context length.
bullets: Needs post-training data representative of your real deployment context lengths
Adds a training/engineering step that training-free sparsity methods skip entirely
Best justified when you're already pushing very long contexts at a tight compute budget
Code and weights are public — Tencent-Hunyuan/Simple-Attention-Sparsification

questions.prompt: What core problem does SAS solve compared to distillation-based sparse-attention selectors?
options: It removes the need for any post-training step
It optimizes context ranking end-to-end with the language-modeling loss instead of imitating dense attention
It only works on sequences shorter than 1,000 tokens
It replaces attention with a recurrent state
questions.explanation: Distillation caps a selector at copying a frozen dense-attention pattern. SAS instead backpropagates the real training objective through continuous gates, so selection is optimized for the task itself.

questions.prompt: What is a 'context unit' in SAS?
options: An individual attention head
An entire document
A contiguous block of tokens
A model layer
questions.explanation: SAS scores and selects blocks of tokens rather than single tokens, which keeps the selection budget-controllable and maps efficiently onto GPU matmul tiling.

questions.prompt: According to the paper, where does SAS show its largest relative improvement over prior baselines?
options: At very loose attention budgets close to full dense attention
At tight attention budgets, i.e. aggressive sparsity
Only during pretraining, never at inference
Only on multimodal benchmarks
questions.explanation: Selection quality matters most when few blocks can be kept — that's exactly where end-to-end optimization of the ranking pays off most over a teacher-imitating selector.
